claims.statement: The OAuth Web App credential (user authentication, a confidential client with an HTTPS redirect) requires the application to store a client secret securely on a backend server and fetch tokens there.

sources.supports: OAuth credentials for Web App require the application to store a client secret on the backend server securely; in OAuth 2.0 terms an OAuth Web App credential is a confidential client with an HTTPS redirect.
The Authentication Guide lists OAuth Web App among the user authentication credential types.

claims.statement: For an OAuth Web App credential (a confidential client) the client secret is presented to the token endpoint in a Basic Authorization header built as Base64(clientId:clientSecret), on the authorization-code token request, the refresh-token request and the token revocation request; the public-client credentials send client_id instead and no secret.

sources.supports: The authorization parameter is required for confidential clients as Authorization: Basic Base64(clientId:clientSecret) on the access-token and refresh requests (the request example for the OAuth Web App credential carries only the Authorization header and the code or refresh_token); the revocation request takes the same header for OAuth Web and OAuth WebApp credentials; client_id is required for public clients.
sources.locator: sections "Fetching Access tokens", "Refreshing Access tokens" and "Token revocation", parameter tables and Web App request examples

claims.statement: The sample OpenID configuration on the same reference page lists client_secret_basic and client_secret_post under token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported; the parameter tables and request examples for the OAuth Web App credential document only the Basic Authorization header form.

The user-authentication pages show the client secret only inside the placeholder expression Base64(clientId:clientSecret) and the placeholder {AUTHORIZATION}; no page read gives an example secret value or states a prefix, alphabet, length or checksum for it.

sources.supports: Request examples use {AUTHORIZATION}; the parameter tables describe the header as Base64(clientId:clientSecret); no value format is stated.
sources.locator: sections "Fetching Access tokens" and "Refreshing Access tokens"

sources.supports: States that the application stores a client secret on the backend server; gives no format for it.

notes: Project-authored by the Redact Secret project, which maintains this repository; not independent evidence. Draft; not yet reviewed. Re-read 2026-10-05: the existing claim is unchanged and three claims about the token-request carrier and the absence of a documented format are added. The p8e- prefix recorded for another family is deliberately not copied here: no source attributes it to this credential type.

openQuestions.question: Adobe documentation read for this candidate gives no prefix, alphabet, length or other format rule for this value; any example in it is a placeholder or a public identifier. Not researched beyond existence.

Whether this client secret has the same shape as the OAuth Server-to-Server client secret is not stated in the pages read. The Single Page App and Native App credentials are public clients that hold no client secret, so they are not candidates.

Whether an Adobe client secret beginning p8e- (treated as an Adobe client secret, type unnamed, by two scanner rule artifacts; see the OAuth Server-to-Server contract) can be an OAuth Web App client secret is not established; the provider pages read do not mention the prefix. Settled by an Adobe statement tying the prefix to a credential type.

The pages read do not state how many client secrets a Web App credential can hold, whether the secret is shown once, or how it is rotated or revoked (the rotation pages found cover the Server-to-Server and Enterprise Web App credentials). Settled by an Adobe page on Web App credential management.

The Basic Authorization header carries the secret inside a Base64 encoding of clientId:clientSecret, so the header value is a representation that contains the secret rather than the secret itself; whether a decoded header is in scope for detection is a downstream decision, and the header's own Base64 form is not an Adobe-stated credential format.
